VERDICT P01 NOT-SUPPORTED — (1) holds: the quote "Shinsatsu are a type of thaumaturgic talisman (also known as gofu) distributed at shrines and symbolic of a spiritual being or its supranormal power" appears verbatim in the article body ("Text" section, with only a space before the closing parenthesis in "gofu )"); (2) fails: this Kokugakuin Digital Museum article on Shinsatsu/Mamorifuda never mentions Pliny or any therapeutic/apotropaic/exorcistic jobs — searches for "Pliny", "therapeutic", "apotropaic", "exorcistic", "first century CE", "heal", "ward" and "exorcism" all return nothing on the page; (3) fails: the entry claims "since Pliny's account in the first century CE, amulets were worn and used for therapeutic, apotropaic or exorcistic benefit, so the same worn object can heal, ward off or drive out", none of which appears anywhere on this page.

VERDICT P02 SUPPORTED — "Iatromancy (busui 卜祟 ) was a method of divination and related techniques used to diagnose and treat illnesses." The quote is verbatim body text ("This method aimed to identify the demons that caused the ailments and expel them through sacrifices, incantations, talismans, and other exorcistic rituals."); it carries the teaches: in the Tang treatment the article reconstructs (Wei Wu, "Terrifying Demons: A Tang-Dynasty Treatment for Demonic Infestation"), talismans figure among the exorcistic means — sacrifices, incantations, talismans, other exorcistic rituals — used to name and expel the demon behind an ailment; it carries every entry claim: the page states iatromancy, in the Tang-dynasty context ("Many iatromantic writings of the Tang dynasty were discovered in Dunhuang"), aimed to identify the demons that caused ailments and expel them through sacrifices, incantations, talismans and other exorcistic rituals.

VERDICT P03 SUPPORTED — "They are invested with the power to heal or protect." The quote is verbatim body text ("Yet most importantly (as described by Pliny since the first century CE) amulets were worn and used for therapeutic, apotropaic or exorcistic benefit."); it carries the teaches: three distinct jobs — therapeutic, apotropaic, exorcistic benefit; it carries every entry claim: the page names Annie Thwaite as author of "A history of amulets in ten objects", and the statement "Thwaite reports that, as described by Pliny since the first century CE, amulets were worn and used for therapeutic, apotropaic or exorcistic benefit" matches the page sentence.

VERDICT P04 SUPPORTED — "Such boxes were worn suspended on a strap or sash across the shoulder or around the waist when travelling." The quote is verbatim body text of the V&A record ("This amulet case or ga'u of silver and coral, was used to hold rolled prayers and blessed or holy objects believed to protect the wearer from evil."); it carries the teaches and the entry claim verbatim: the record describes this amulet case or ga'u as used to hold rolled prayers and blessed or holy objects believed to protect the wearer from evil (object: Amulet Box (ga'u), Tibet, 1800–1850).

VERDICT P05 SUPPORTED — "or hung on a wall, and could also be wrapped around the body of the deceased as a form of prayer." The quote is verbatim body text of the item record ("Inscribed with healing prayers, talismans, and images of armed angels, amulet scrolls like this one might be placed in a leather case to be worn"); it carries the teaches: the scroll carries healing prayers, talismans and armed angels and can be placed in a leather case worn on the body; it carries every entry claim: the page describes this Ethiopian amulet scroll as inscribed with healing prayers, talismans and images of armed angels and placed in a leather case to be worn, and as inscribed with healing prayers, talismans and images of armed angels.

VERDICT P06 NOT-SUPPORTED — (1) holds, hyphenation aside: the page reads "In five of the printed D charms, the amulet consists of a writing con- taining mysterious words, letters, and other symbols" (line-break hyphen in "containing"); (2) holds: the page (Grendon, Anglo-Saxon Charms) carries the teaches that the amulet in these D charms consists of a writing of mysterious words, letters and symbols; (3) fails: the entry adds a second claim — "the custom spread from eighteenth-century Lima through the Pacific trade" — which appears nowhere on this page (searches for "Lima", "Pacific" and "eighteenth" all return nothing), so the entry is not fully carried by the page.

VERDICT P07 SUPPORTED — "And in the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki there is an Icon of the Virgin Hodegetria that is hung with votives from St. Menas at Dragoumi and Agiou Mina." The quote is verbatim body text ("In addition to holy icons and unorthodox amulets, there survive icons in the amuletic form of engraved stones to be worn on the body."); it carries the teaches: some surviving icons were engraved stones in amuletic form for wearing on the body, alongside holy icons and unorthodox amulets; it carries the entry claim verbatim: icons survive in the amuletic form of engraved stones to be worn on the body, alongside holy icons and unorthodox amulets.

VERDICT P08 SUPPORTED — "Carthaginian excavations traced the open hand to ancient Egypt, whose variations appear across all faiths and time as a representation of God and believed to grant protection against ill will." The quote is verbatim body text of the Description field ("Jewish silversmiths in Morocco became known for casting and engraving pieces such as this one, used as a talismanic doorknob or jewellery pendant."); it carries the teaches: Moroccan Jewish silversmiths cast and engraved hand-shaped amulets (this object is the "Hand of Fatima"/Khamsa; the page calls silver's role there "amuletic power") used as talismanic doorknobs or jewellery pendants; it carries every entry claim: the page states Moroccan Jewish silversmiths cast and engraved hand pieces used as a talismanic doorknob or jewellery pendant, and that Jewish silversmiths in Morocco became known for casting and engraving talismanic hand pieces.
